analytic.title: SAC-tool: a tool for scheduling analysis and correction of multiprocessor Real Time Systems

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: For several years, real time systems (RTS) have been continuously growing and complex. The time needed for their development is consequently very important and their accuracy is crucial for human and economic disaster prevention. In this vein, scheduling analysis and correction at the early stage of RTS application life cycle can effectively reduce potential scheduling faults (temporal faults). Thus, reduce the important cost, risk and effort of development. However, despite the diversity of scheduling analysis techniques, they can only detect the schedulability of an RTS without the proposal of possible correction, if the system is detected non-schedulable. Existing scheduling analysis techniques lack autonomy, so require other rigorous means (tools) to assist them in correction. It is then recommended to integrate into scheduling analysis techniques a method for correction to ensure autonomy and to save time and effort. In this paper we present a prototype of the SAC-tool (Scheduling analysis and correction tool) implementing a new method of scheduling analysis and correction dedicated for multiprocessor RTS. To illustrate and extend this method a static view via UML class diagram is presented in this paper. Two main steps are provided in SAC-tool, a configuration editing step and a scheduling analysis and correction step.

div.head: I. INTRODUCTION
div.p: Powerful architectures, such as multiprocessor and multicores architectures [1,2] are widely used for real-time scheduling [3,4]. In fact, a variety of research studies are undertaken in this field, among which the projection of an RTS application on multiprocessor architecture [5,6] is the most crucial.

The literature on multiprocessor scheduling shows two main scheduling families, the global and the partitioned family [9]. In the global family there is no assignment of tasks to processors, since each task can migrate all over available processors. Nevertheless, the migration and preemption require important costs [7,8], which can eventually affect the scheduling results [12].

Contrary to the global family, the partitioned family requires two main steps [13]. The first is the assignment phase, in which the tasks are distributed over the processors. In fact, in this family once a task is assigned to a processor, its migration is forbidden. Each partition scheduling problem is then treated separately. Thus, the preemption and migration costs are decreased [10]. The second step is the scheduling analysis phase [14,15], in which the RTS schedulability is checked. Indeed, to satisfy the timing constraints, this step must be carried out at an early stage during the development life cycle. Thus, the system temporal behavior can be distinguished from the beginning and the possible eventual risks can be spotted [16].

It is worthy to mention that, once detected, it is very important to correct the scheduling faults. However, the costs of correction are very important. In fact, when detecting a non-schedulable configuration, the only corrective action is limited to the regenerating of a new (NP-hard) partitioning solution [17,18]. This regeneration is time consuming and complex.

As some existing works focuses on the partitioning quality [19,20], as the only corrective action to reduce the risk of non-schedulable configurations. Others, focuses on the scheduling analysis quality [16] to save time and effort. Indeed, the literature on scheduling analysis shows a variety of techniques, which some results are still in progress, such as analytical techniques, simulation techniques [22], and other more secure formal techniques [16,23]. Proving the correctness of a schedule for some of these techniques, is limited to verifying if any deadline is missed until the hyperperiod [40]. Hence, if a system can be scheduled for one hyper-period [41] and sometimes two [42], it can be scheduled for all. However, for most works, this scheduling analysis remains necessary but not sufficient [43]. Moreover, it is limited to detecting the non schedulability without proposing a concrete correction solution.

Even though the efficiency of these scheduling analysis solutions has been improved in recent years, most improvements have been achieved by enhancing the detection part. That's to say, when exploring a system, it's about judging correctly its schedulability. However, this action does not correct the RTS non-schedulable partitions.

Actually, the studies that precise the details of the nonschedulable partitions (exceeding-partitions, exceedingtasks) if the system is non-schedulable, are still lacking. In the best of our knowledge, the most interesting formal approach to this issue has been proposed by [16].

In fact, in this work [16], a description of the nonschedulable partitions is established to improve the feedback quality. This feedback is useful to generate new feasible partitions [24] and reduce the space solutions exploration. It is true that this work improves the scheduling analysis quality and can reduce the time and effort of the NP-hard partitioning regenerations. Nonetheless it is possible to further improve the efficiency by assuring furthermore the correction. Thus, minimize the consumed amount of time of the back and forth to the partitioning-tool. However, in the best of our knowledge, very few publications are available in the literature that address the issue of scheduling correction [21].

In a recent paper [21], a new method for scheduling analysis and correction of periodic RTS with tasks migration, is presented. This method aims to accelerate the process of finding a schedulable solution. In fact, it works on reducing the non-schedulable configurations by correcting them with task migration. Thus, instead of returning to the partitioningtool for a new configuration regeneration, the correction is made locally in the middle of the scheduling analysis.

In fact, the correction method in [21] is based on migrating some tasks from the overloaded processors, toward the not loaded ones. Thus, instead of regenerating a new configuration, the non-schedulable one is, if possible, rectified. Hence, in this work [21], the migrant tasks are not necessarily, the tasks having exceeded their deadlines. It is about migrating the tasks having the minimum task load [21] and affecting them in their best-fit from the target processors.

The main purpose of this paper, is the extension of the work presented in [21]. In fact, we aim to propose a tool dedicated for both of the scheduling analysis and correction (SAC-tool). Moreover, we try to prove it through experimentation.

The reminder of this paper is organized as follows into seven sections, section II outlines the existing scheduling analysis principles and its major problems. Section III, discusses a new method of scheduling correction and its drawbacks. In, Section IV a static view via an UML class model is proposed and discussed in order to improve the method in [21]. In fact, the given class model constitutes an entry point for developing an autonomous tool dedicated for both of the scheduling analysis and correction of a multiprocessor RTS called SAC-tool. The architecture of the SAC-tool prototype is presented in section V. In section VI, some case studies are performed to validate and investigate the proposed approach. The conclusion is reported in section VII.

div.head: II. SCHEDULING ANALYSIS
div.p: The scheduling analysis step has been always challenging for RTS. The literature on multiprocessor scheduling analysis, shows a variety of techniques [15,16,28]. Thus, the choice of the appropriate scheduling family is an important step, that requires a vast knowledge of the scheduling field.

In multiprocessor RTS scheduling, the global family is far from being used in the practice due to its time-consuming migration and preemption [4,28,29]. This is what favored the partitioned family to be more predominant in practice [21,26,27]. In fact, although this latter is not adapted to dynamism it seems to be stronger because it solves global scheduling problems, starting from the lack of migration cost and going to the scheduling optimality [4,30,31].

In fact, the scheduling analysis in partitioned family consists in analyzing each partition separately. Indeed, it is a question of adapting the well-known mono-processor schedulability analysis methods [32] to each processor apart, in a multiprocessor context. Thus, this family seems to always have an advantage compared to the best feasibility tests of the global scheduling [4]. However, the major problem in this family is the risk of non-schedulable partitions. In fact, if the schedulability analysis detects nonschedulability, it is sometimes desirable to partition a task across multiple processors to be able to schedule the task system and relax the induced overload. Unfortunately, partitioned family does not allow that. For this reason, once the schedulability analysis detect non-schedulable partitions, it is necessary to turn into the partitioning tool for corrective actions. In this case a new partitioning solution is regenerated and the schedulability analysis needs to start again. Nevertheless, as said above, the RTS partitioning problem is most often a (NP-hard) problem [17,18]. Consequently, such regeneration can lead to a very important time cost till reaching schedulability.

A lot of schedulability analysis techniques were distinguished for the partitioned family. In [9], an assessment of major existing results in this area based on the number of sets of tasks that are detected to be schedulable. This assessment showed that the overall schedulability tests improved significantly. However, they are incomparable in terms of sets of schedulable tasks detected. Also, they are limited compared to the amount of extra calculation needed (complexity). Indeed, despite the diversity of scheduling analysis techniques, they remain insufficient. In fact, these techniques are only detection ones, without the proposal of possible corrections [9,13]. Thus, they are generally, not autonomous and require other means (tools) to assist them in correcting the system eventual faults. However, only few of them are assisted by a tool due to their delicacy and complexity [12,18,33]. So, it is very interesting to integrate into them, methods for correction to ensure autonomy and to save time and effort.

div.head: III. SCHEDULING CORRECTION
div.p: Quite recently, considerable attention has been paid to scheduling correction [21,24], due to its important and direct impact for a better schedulability in the practice.

In [21], a new partitioning and analyzing method dedicated to correct the non-schedulable partitions and to avoid the regeneration cost [25]. This latter, present a scheduling correction solution that may be integrated into the scheduling analysis. In fact, if the RTS is detected nonschedulable, this method rectifies the partitioning on the bases of the migration of some independent tasks from the loaded processor called "source" toward their best fit from the not loaded once called "target". In this method, the correction of the partitioning is done locally into the considered configuration without the need of the back and forth to the partitioning-tool [22]. Analytical verification is provided to check the partitions due to its polynomial complexity [31]. Indeed, in [21] load calculation is key to predict the schedulability. In the bases of this calculation, the partitions sources of temporal faults can be detected. Then a relaxing of them based on the task migration principle [34] can lead to an actual correction while promoting reducing the temporal costs.

The continuous need for scheduling correction to avoid system failures and to save time and effort has become more challenging mainly without a tool dedicated for this purpose. In this respect, this paper was proposed to deal with the automation of the scheduling analysis and correction. A prototype of a tool called SAC-tool was prepared to allow checking the temporal behavior and correcting the RTS configurations automatically.

The correction in [21] is based only on the task-level migration principle. Indeed, correction results depending only on this level are reduced due to processor space issues [33] and partitioning issues [17,18]. In this paper, when referring to this earlier work [21], the focus is different. We try to handle all the correction levels (job-level, portionedjob-level) [44], to enhance the probability of correction. For this end a general UML class structure will be presented to highlight these aspects. Moreover, some interfaces of SAC tool developed for this purpose will be presented to concretize and to enhance this correction method.

div.head: IV. UML CLASS MODEL FOR SCHEDULING ANALYSIS AND CORRECTION METHOD
div.p: The Unified Modeling Language (UML) class diagram [35] can be a good fit for modeling the new method of scheduling analysis and correction of multiprocessor RTS presented in [21]. In fact, UML and Extensible Markup Language (XML) [36] are the bases later for the development of a tool for scheduling analysis and correction (SAC-tool). Actually, UML class model can be a good fit for giving a rich general structure of the targeted method. Moreover, the data existing in the latter class diagram can be interchanged to a portable xml structure.

In "Fig. 1", all the classes, associations, dependencies, interfaces and some constraints needed are used to summaries this structure. It serves also to build the associated SAC-tool interfaces and to develop the associated algorithm. Indeed, it is obvious that an RTS-configuration is composed of a set of tasks and partitions. The tasks have temporal properties and can be either dependent or not. The method in [21] is dedicated for independent tasks. Thus, it can be presented with the black structure in the figure. This method is enriched by the rest of the red structure for future works (dependent task correction, thread migration). The execution of a dependent task is conditioned with precedence. The tasks can be composed also of a set of threads which are hardly dependent. The allocation of tasks to partition is presented with an association class called "allocation".

The kernel of the scheduling analysis and correction algorithm, is decomposed into methods associated to the concerned classes. Mainly, the "Check_Partitons()" associated to the "allocaion" class that uses also the " calculate_load() " method from the "Partitions" class. This latter is needed to classify them into "source", "target", and "blocked" partitions. They are respectively, the overloaded once where some tasks exceeded deadlines, the not loaded once candidate for migration, and the on-load limit once which cannot support other tasks. the analytical formula for calculating the load can be found in [21]. Other important method presented, is the "extract_all_migratory_tasks()". It works actually on the "source", partitions in order to find the tasks candidate for migration "migratory_tasks" to assure the correction of the schedule on each source partition. The principle of this method can be found in [21]. The actual "RTS_correction()" method is limited to correcting the partitioning with independent task migration. In fact, the task-level correction approach seen in [21,23], has the major limits of not being able to partition a task if no target processor can receive it as a whole. Whereas, if the task is partitioned into slices (bin-packing) [37,38,39] over the existing target processors while respecting precedence, it can then be corrected. Thus, the thread level and the dependent tasks for the actual scheduling temporal correction will be treated in future works. This is what justifies the existence of the additional classes and associations illustrated in red in "Fig. 1", (migratory threads, thread, dependent_tasks, and the recursive associations, task_precedence and thread_precedence to illustrate the dependency relations between tasks and threads [16,21]).

div.head: V. SAC-TOOL ARCHITECTURE
div.p: The functional architecture of SAC-tool is shown in ("Fig. 2"), ("Fig. 3"). Actually, it is decomposed into two parts, the first is the editing part ("Fig. 2"), and the second is the execution part ("Fig. 3").

The first part of SAC-tool is required to initialize the attributes necessary for creating an RTS configuration. In fact, the set of tasks of each processor is initialized with its temporal characteristics ("Fig. 4").

. The description of all processors partitions is then serialized as an xml file. The generated xml file conforms to our class model structure presents the entry port point to the scheduling analysis and correction executer.
In fact, once the RTS configuration is edited to the SACtool interface, we need to easily extract the existing data from it. An intermediate extraction step is then required.

Fortunately, parsing the generated xml file, allows extracting all the configuration information. Thus, for each processor, its assigned tasks and temporal characteristics is easily distinguished. Hence, since the extraction of all necessary data can be realized from the xml file, the execution part can then be lunched to supply the schedulability checking and correcting. The execution part of the edited configuration can give then the result of the scheduling analysis ("Fig. 5"), and correction ("Fig. 6"). In fact, based on analytical computation of the processor loads [21], the scheduling_analysis is performed. In the case of non-schedulable configurations, the scheduling_correction step is lunched. Once the correction is realized the initial configuration stored in the xml file is rectified not regenerated.

div.head: VI. SAC-TOOL EXPERIMENTATION
div.p: In this section, we present a demonstration of the SACtool through 2 case studies.

In fact, we introduce two non-schedulable RTS and we detail the steps to correct these systems based on the proposed approach in [21]. The studied cases, highlight synchronous real-time task system (ri = 0) running on identical processors (homogenous). These case studies can match with real time applications, where the execution is done off-line and the dovetailing is done on-line (distributed system).

The first case study deals with 13 independent tasks running on 4 identical processors. The specifications of the task characteristics and their allocation to processors are described in "TABLE I" as follows.

div.p: The system is at the beginning not schedulable because the partitions P1 and P4 are superior to 1.
Thus, the migratory tasks on the processor source P4 are respectively, (T3, T13) and on the processor source P1 (T6, T4).
All the migratory task structure after contain respectively (T13, T4, T6, T3).
The Migration steps needed are:
• T13 to the target processor P3 (U3 becomes 0.6833)
• T4 to the target processor P3 (U3 becomes 0.9833)
• T6 to the target processor P2 (U2 becomes 0.9277)
• T3 to the target processor P2 (U2 becomes 0.9848)

The final capacity of processors is respectively, (U1=0.9, U2=0.9848, U3=0.9833, U4=0.9) So, after 4 migration steps the system becomes schedulable. The correction is efficient for this system. however, sometimes alternative choices for the migration tasks can reduce more the migration costs, for example if we chose to migrate the task T1 (task_load= 0.4) from the processor P1 toward the processor P3, then the correction of the processor is done with only one step instead of two. The migration cost can then be reduced. (Updates on the algorithm proposed on [21] can be the focus in future works).

The second case study deals with 11 independent tasks running on 5 identical processors. The specifications of the task characteristics and their allocation to processors are described in "TABLE II" as follows. The initial capacity of processors is respectively, (U1 = 1.1952, U2= 1,1315, U3=0.6015, U4=1.6717, U5=0.4173).
Thus, the migratory tasks on the processor source P1 is (T2), on the processor source P2 is (T3), on the processor source P4 are respectively (T9, T7).
All the migratory task structure after contain respectively (T7, T2, T9, T3).
The Migration steps needed are:
• T7 to the target processor P5 (U5 becomes 0.9294)
• T2 to the target processor P3 (U3 becomes 0.8422)
• T9 to the target processor P3 (U3 becomes 1.0313)
• T3 to the target processor P5 (U5 becomes 1.1136)

The final capacity of processors is respectively, (U1=0.9545, U2=0.9473, U3=1.0313, U4=1.1596, U5=1.1136) So, after 4 migration steps the system remain nonschedulable. However, if at some level of the migration we partitioned the tasks T9 and T3 on the rest of the available processors P1 which became target after the migration (T2 to P3) and on P5, the system could be corrected. However, the method in [21] does not allow that. That's why (Updates on the algorithm proposed on [21] can be the focus in future works).

The case study used in the screen shots ("Fig. 4", "Fig. 5" "Fig. 6") to check the usability and the efficiency of SACtool is the one proposed in [21]. The case study 1 and 2 was simulated also on SAC-tool. The simulation results match the calculations.

Other cases were also treated [23]. This case treats specific cases where the overload on the processor, matches exactly a load of some migrant tasks. However, this is far from being true. The simulation of this case with the method in [21] on the SAC-tool was checked.
Sometimes we have met, invalid corrections, due to the previous limitation of the scheduling analysis and correction method [21] based on task migration algorithm announced earlier in this paper.

The use of the SAC-tool makes it easier and faster to edit, check and correct an RTS configuration. So, it is sufficient for the user to edit an RTS configuration to be automatically checked and corrected. In fact, SAC-tool is an effective way to achieve a fast scheduling analysis and to correct the nonschedulable partitions without the regeneration of a new ones. In fact, the results of the analysis and correction are provided very quickly. SAC-tool, has fixed so far, the inability to give a reliable partitioning solution from the beginning. This can explain why this scheduling analysis and correction method can be very used in practice. For this reason, we intend to evaluate the results of our tool continuously during our future researches. In this work, we tried to automate both the analysis and correction of an RTS without the need for other means (tools) for assistance. For this purpose, this paper explores the development of an autonomous tool (SAC-toll) implementing a new scheduling analysis and correction method. This method is able to check and correct the partitioning with task migration if needed. Actually, it saves time and effort by minimizing the back and forth to the partitioning tool for new partitioning solution regeneration.

Actually, we have proposed an UML class model to present a static overview of the method and to enrich it for future work. In fact, the given class model constitutes an entry point for developing an autonomous tool dedicated for both of scheduling analysis and correction for multiprocessor RTS called SAC-tool.

In fact, during this study, we used the SAC-tool to validate some experimentation. In relevant cases, configurations were corrected not regenerated. In some other cases, we have found that the correction in task-level is insufficient.

Actually, it is true that the migration cost in task-level is less consuming. However, based on this principle, the correction results are reduced given the problems of the lack of processor space. Moreover, task-level migration, prevents the partitioning of tasks. However, partitioning a task (dividing into threads) can more frequently correct the RTS temporal faults. Thus, it is very interesting to improve the correction approach to be able to divide the execution of tasks on multiple processors, or cores (job-level-migration). Further study to this issue would be of interest.

For this purpose, we intend to improve SAC-tool in future studies, with a more rigorous and autonomous algorithm for scheduling analysis and correction, that touches all the correction levels (tasks, threads and even portions).

We have considered in this work an RTS composed of a set of periodic independent tasks to validate the proposed scheduling analysis and correction approach. However, tasks are hardly dependent, especially in critical RTS, which are more often real applications, such as control of nuclear power stations, robotics, avionics, communication, etc.
Clearly further research will be needed to validate and stabilize the SAC-tool and to prove its applicability in real applications.
